target: AG1’s opening case that AI can improve everyday convenience, health, learning/work productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety, and thus is good for society
objection: AI systems often rely on large-scale personal-data collection and profiling, which creates serious privacy risks such as unintended disclosure, surveillance-like profiling, and downstream misuse; those privacy harms can also produce social and economic costs and chill participation.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps marginalized groups and society broadly
objection: When AI is trained on biased data, it can reproduce discriminatory patterns and worsen outcomes for racial minorities and other targeted groups, so AI can exacerbate racism and racial inequality.

target: AG1’s claim that AI makes work easier and beneficial for students/professionals
objection: AI automation can displace or devalue workers’ tasks and shift profits and power toward large firms, harming the economic well-being of many people and businesses.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps students and professionals
objection: AI tools can reduce users’ need to practice thinking, explaining, and verifying for themselves, which can undermine critical thinking skills for students and adults.

target: AG1’s idea that privacy, bias, economic disruption, and critical-thinking harms can be mitigated through responsible deployment
objection: The safeguards AG1 relies on are not reliably carried out at scale because firms have incentives to prioritize performance, growth, and revenue; therefore AI deployments do not reliably and substantially eliminate privacy and misuse risks.

target: AG1’s claim that bias mitigation can substantially reduce discriminatory outputs
objection: Bias mitigation and audits are not reliably effective in practice because discriminatory outputs can re-emerge from changing real-world data, changing contexts, and the limits of audits, so AI can still exacerbate racism and racial inequality.

target: AG1’s claim that reskilling, redeployment, and AI-as-tutor designs can avoid economic disruption and critical-thinking erosion
objection: Broad AI adoption tends to move faster than labor-market support can scale, and in everyday use many people will treat AI as a shortcut, so economic insecurity and critical-thinking erosion persist rather than being fully prevented.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy, discrimination, economic, and educational harms are not dominant if mitigations work
objection: Even under AG1’s governance framing, AI still generates serious privacy harms, and if those harms remain significant they can dominate the overall societal impact for many people, making AI not good for society.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy risks alone do not determine AI’s social verdict
objection: Serious privacy and misuse risks directly harm autonomy and basic control over personal life, and they also chill participation in public and economic life, so privacy harms can be socially decisive on their own.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy harms can be designed away by limited data sharing
objection: Even with user-provided inputs or local processing, health, learning, and accessibility AI still requires sensitive information and can still infer sensitive traits; local or limited-data designs do not reliably eliminate serious privacy and misuse risks.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving architecture prevents participation-chilling
objection: Even privacy-preserving AI can still leave serious privacy risks in place, and those risks can still make people avoid or reduce engagement with AI-mediated services, undermining the benefits AG1 cites.

target: AG1’s claim that consent, opt-out, and deletion give users meaningful control and prevent chilling
objection: In many deployments those controls are opaque or partial, so users cannot reliably stop logging, secondary use, third-party analytics, or incomplete deletion; as a result, privacy concerns can still cause participation-chilling.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be designed to reduce racial bias and critical-thinking erosion
objection: AI trained on social data can generate biased outputs and, because users tend to rely on fluent answers, AI use can reduce independent verification and reasoning, thereby amplifying racism and undermining critical thinking.

target: AG1’s claim that fairness-aware training, curated data, and independent bias audits can substantially reduce discriminatory outputs
objection: Bias-mitigation measures are inherently limited because models and contexts change after deployment, so biased outputs can re-emerge even after audits and mitigation.

target: AG1’s claim that verification prompts and uncertainty cues can preserve critical thinking and reduce reliance on biased outputs
objection: Even with uncertainty labels and citations, many users still treat fluent AI outputs as authoritative and do not meaningfully verify them, so prompts do not reliably stop reliance on biased content.

target: AG1’s claim that AI in education can support critical thinking when used as feedback and practice
objection: In typical classroom and home use, AI is time-saving and answer-generating, and without strong enforcement many learners offload thinking to the system, which reduces practice in critical evaluation.

target: AG1’s claim that human-in-the-loop review prevents biased AI outputs from causing discrimination
objection: In practice, decision-makers often rely on fluent AI suggestions as decision aids, so formally retained human responsibility does not reliably stop biased outputs from influencing real-world decisions.

target: AG1’s claim that efficient review procedures can handle high-volume settings
objection: High-volume or time-constrained settings make substantive human review difficult, so review often becomes cursory and discriminatory errors can still slip through.

target: AG1’s claim that structured workflows can keep AI from worsening racism
objection: Biased AI outputs can still influence surrounding steps such as drafted rationales, suggested questions, summaries, and everyday communications, where the same verification discipline is not enforced, so structured workflows at final decision points do not stop broader amplification and normalization of stereotypes.

target: AG1’s claim that workflow-wide approval and content controls can block biased propagation
objection: Those controls miss implicit bias, because discrimination can show up through latent associations, framing, and ranking/recommendation differences without any obvious stereotype phrase for filters or reviewers to catch.

target: AG1’s claim that outcome-based fairness testing can detect and reduce implicit discriminatory effects
objection: Outcome-based fairness evaluation only measures specific metrics under specific test conditions and can miss broader racism harms such as stereotype reinforcement and downstream unequal treatment in untested contexts.

target: AG1’s claim that broader scenario coverage and continuous monitoring can address what narrow tests miss
objection: Continuous post-deployment monitoring typically requires detailed linkage of user interactions, outcomes, and demographic or proxy data, which increases surveillance-like profiling and sensitive personal-data use and creates additional privacy harms.

target: AG1’s claim that continuous monitoring and enforcement can keep AI net-positive
objection: Monitoring and enforcement only work after enough real-world outcomes have accumulated to detect disparities, so biased AI can still operate and cause discriminatory harm during the detection lag, and later corrections cannot undo the harm already incurred.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy harms make AI deployments dangerous because responsible deployment cannot reliably control data use
objection: The privacy harms AG2 highlights depend heavily on deployment choices; privacy-preserving practices such as data minimization, encryption, strict access controls, auditing, consent and retention limits can substantially reduce misuse pathways.

target: AG2’s claim that AI exacerbates racism because biased outputs are learned from biased data
objection: Discriminatory outputs can be substantially reduced through curated or balanced datasets, bias-aware training, independent testing and audits, and human review for high-stakes uses.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily causes economic disruption and critical-thinking erosion
objection: Those harms depend on deployment choices, and they can be lessened through workforce transition supports like reskilling and redeployment plus educational designs that use AI as a tutor while requiring reasoning and verification.

target: AG2’s claim that governance and compliance cannot reliably prevent serious privacy and misuse risks
objection: Organizations face real governance pressures—legal compliance, audits, contractual obligations, and reputational or liability incentives—that make privacy and safety controls actionable in many mainstream deployments rather than optional.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy harms alone can determine the societal verdict on AI
objection: Whether AI is good for society depends on its overall net effects on safety, health, learning, work, and accessibility, not on privacy harms alone.

target: AG2’s claim that limited data sharing and local processing do not reduce privacy chilling
objection: Many AI benefits can be delivered with limited sensitive-data sharing, using user-provided inputs, anonymized or aggregated data, or local/on-device processing, which reduces the chance that privacy worries will chill participation.

target: AG2’s claim that even local processing cannot prevent privacy harms
objection: If systems are designed with privacy-preserving architecture—local inference, no persistent raw-data retention, encryption, limited telemetry, and differential privacy or federated updates with anti-secondary-use limits—then inference and downstream misuse pathways can be substantially reduced.

target: AG2’s claim that consent, opt-out, and deletion cannot prevent chilling
objection: Meaningful user agency through clear consent, easy opt-out, and the ability to limit or delete data use can reduce the extent to which privacy concerns deter people from using AI-supported services.

target: AG2’s claim that AI will reproduce racial bias and reduce verification and critical thinking
objection: Fairness-aware training, curated and representative datasets, and independent bias audits can substantially reduce discriminatory outputs, and AI can be designed to encourage verification by showing uncertainty, citing sources, and prompting confirmation for high-stakes uses.

target: AG2’s claim that human-in-the-loop review does not stop biased AI from influencing decisions
objection: Structured workflows can reduce reliance on fluent suggestions by displaying uncertainty, providing evidence tied to inputs, and requiring humans to document independent justifications before acting.

target: AG2’s claim that AI outputs inevitably spread bias in surrounding steps
objection: Organizations can extend controls beyond final decisions by requiring human approval before AI-authored communications are sent, mandating source/citation display, labeling outputs as drafts, and checking content to prevent biased propagation.

target: AG2’s claim that outcome-based fairness evaluation misses harmful bias
objection: Broader scenario coverage, counterfactual and red-team testing, and continuous post-deployment monitoring with corrective actions can detect and reduce discriminatory influence beyond narrow test metrics.

target: AG2’s claim that monitoring itself creates unacceptable privacy harms
objection: Although monitoring uses more data, those privacy costs do not automatically outweigh the discrimination-reduction benefits, so monitoring can still improve the overall social outcome.

target: AG2’s claim that monitoring lags make net-positive outcomes impossible
objection: Responsible deployment can use staged rollouts, throttling, guardrails, and rapid rollback so that biased outputs are limited quickly rather than allowed to persist for a long lag period.
